concept.name: Maximum drawdown
concept.definition: The largest observed peak-to-trough decline of an equity or NAV series over an evaluation period, usually quoted as a percentage of the running peak. Formally it is the maximum of the drawdown process over the sample.
concept.intuition: It is the worst pain the strategy has actually inflicted: the deepest hole from peak to trough that an investor would have had to sit through.
concept.mechanics: Scan the equity curve keeping a running peak, compute the percentage decline from that peak at every point, and take the maximum. It is a single-observation statistic driven by the worst episode in the window.
concept.formula: MDD(T) = max_{tau in (0,T)} [ max_{t in (0,tau)} X(t) - X(tau) ], commonly expressed as a percentage of max_{t in (0,tau)} X(t).
concept.failure_modes: MDD grows with sample length and is dominated by one event, making it an unstable estimator of tail risk; a backtest without a severe episode shows a deceptively small MDD. For a positive-drift process, expected MDD grows with time, so MDDs across different horizons are not comparable.
concept.misconceptions: MDD is not 'the most you can lose' going forward — future drawdowns can exceed the historical maximum — and it is not necessarily the drawdown that lasted longest.
concept.example: If an equity curve runs 100 -> 130 -> 91 -> 140, the maximum drawdown is (130 - 91) / 130 = 30%, even though the series later makes new highs.
